t: LeetCode 2155 — All Divisions With the Highest Score of a Binary Array
o: We may cut the binary array nums at any boundary i from 0 to n: the left part nums[0..i-1] and the right part nums[i..n-1], either of which may be empty. The division score of i is (number of 0s on the left) + (number of 1s on the right), and we must return every index attaining the maximum score. In Example 1, nums = [0,0,1,0]: split 2 leaves [0,0] on the left and [1,0] on the right for a score of 2 + 1 = 3, and split 4 puts everything on the left for 3 + 0 = 3, so [2,4] is the answer. Example 3, nums = [1,1], peaks at split 0 because both 1s stay on the right. With n up to 10^5 there are n+1 candidate cuts, so recounting both sides per cut (quadratic) is off the table; anything built on prefixes or a single sweep is comfortably fast.
k: The score changes by exactly ±1 when the split advances past one element: +1 for a 0 joining the left side, −1 for a 1 leaving the right side.
The split at index 0 has score equal to the total count of 1s, giving a free starting point for a sweep.
All n+1 split positions are candidates — including the two empty-side extremes — and every tie must be reported.

a.i: Directly simulate the definition: try all n+1 split points and recount zeros on the left and ones on the right each time. It is the most literal reading of the statement and trivially correct, but the double rescan makes it quadratic — too slow once n reaches 10^5, though valuable as a correctness baseline.
s: For every split index i from 0 to n, scan nums[:i] counting zeros and nums[i:] counting ones.
Track the maximum score seen so far.
Reset the answer list on a strictly better score; extend it on a tie.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of the n+1 splits both sides are rescanned
a.sp: O(1) extra — only counters aside from the output list

a.i: Adjacent splits differ only at the boundary element, so precomputation kills the rescanning. Counting how many zeros lie before each index and how many ones lie at-or-after each index lets us evaluate every split in O(1) after two simple passes.
s: Build zeroLeft[i] = number of 0s in nums[0..i-1] with a forward pass.
Build oneRight[i] = number of 1s in nums[i..n-1] with a backward pass.
Evaluate score(i) = zeroLeft[i] + oneRight[i] for every i and record the maximum.
Collect every index whose score equals the maximum.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes build the counts, one more evaluates all splits
a.sp: O(n) — two count arrays of length n+1

a.i: Even the count arrays are unnecessary. Start with the split at 0, whose score is simply the total number of 1s. Moving the boundary past element nums[i] adds 1 when nums[i]==0 (its zero joins the left side) and removes 1 when nums[i]==1 (that one abandons the right side). One linear sweep with two integers tracks every score exactly.
s: Initialize score = total number of 1s in nums (the score of split 0).
Sweep i from 0 to n-1: add 1 to score if nums[i]==0, else subtract 1.
After processing element i, score equals the score of split i+1.
Keep the running maximum; reset the answer list on improvement and extend it on ties.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to count 1s plus one update pass
a.sp: O(1) — a handful of scalars beyond the output

w: Lead with the incremental sweep — it signals strong prefix-difference intuition. Pitfalls: forgetting split n (empty right side) breaks all-zeros inputs like [0,0,0] where n wins; confusing element position i with split index i+1; and resetting versus extending the answer list on ties. Follow-ups: maximize zeros-left minus ones-right, process the array as a stream, or count optimal splits — all fall to the same ±1 delta argument.
